statement: In two randomized or counterbalanced, double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies of healthy adults, an antidepressant of the SSRI type (a medicine that blocks the serotonin transporter) taken before MDMA lowered the effects that people rated and that were measured; in the one study that took blood samples, the MDMA level was not lower. In 16 volunteers (3 of whom had tried ecstasy before) given citalopram by infusion before MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg), ratings of the altered state that MDMA brings on, taken 2 hours later, were lower on 10 of the 13 item clusters that MDMA had raised, by about 55 to 80 percent (editors' calculation from the printed means; the authors say about 60 percent); the rises in self-confidence and extroversion were lowered, those in emotional excitability and sensitivity were not, and no blood samples were taken (Liechti et al., 2000). In 12 men given paroxetine daily for 3 days before MDMA 100 mg, the rises in systolic pressure (12 mm Hg lower at the peak), heart rate (14 beats a minute lower at the peak, though not by the area test), pupil width (3.33 to 1.23 mm) and temperature (0.3 degrees lower) were smaller, ratings of euphoria, 'high' and liking were lower, ratings of bad effects, fear and low mood did not change, and no serious adverse event occurred; the peak MDMA level was 16% higher (246.6 against 212.7 ug/L), the exposure to 21 hours 22% higher, and the level of its metabolite HMMA 49% lower at the peak and 39% lower in exposure (Farre et al., 2007). As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), a third SSRI, fluoxetine, lowered ratings of liking, 'high' and 'stimulated' in 8 people, and the review reports no serious adverse effects of any of these combinations in the trials. So in the one study that measured it, feeling less came with more MDMA in the blood, not less. Some people feel little from an amount, for reasons that include a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ and, as here, a medicine that blunts the effect, and some of them take more. Neither study gave more MDMA once the effects were blunted, so what happens then was not measured; the authors of the paroxetine study and of a probe-drug study suggest, without testing it, that it could add risk (Farre et al., 2007; O'Mathuna et al., 2008). Both studies used healthy volunteers, one infusion of citalopram or 3 days of paroxetine, and one fixed amount of MDMA by mouth, and the review found no trial in which people had taken an SSRI or a similar medicine for months before MDMA. Other antidepressants, reports of harm and monoamine-oxidase inhibitors are covered in separate claims.
plain: In two lab studies, healthy volunteers who first took an SSRI antidepressant (citalopram or paroxetine) felt much less from MDMA. With citalopram they rated the effects about 60 percent lower; with paroxetine the rises in the upper blood pressure number, heart rate and pupil size were smaller. The MDMA level in the blood was not lower. With paroxetine it was about 1 in 6 higher at the peak, so feeling less did not mean less MDMA in the body (citalopram's blood levels were not measured). Some people feel little from an amount and take more. The reasons can be a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, or a medicine that mutes the effect, as here. No study gave more MDMA to people on an SSRI, so what happens then is not known; the paroxetine authors suggest it could add risk. The volunteers were healthy, had the SSRI for 3 days at most, and got one fixed amount of MDMA.
population: Healthy adult volunteers in two laboratory studies: 16 people in Zurich (12 men, 4 women; 3 had tried ecstasy, 13 had not) and 12 men in Barcelona (all with earlier MDMA use and normal CYP2D6 function), screened for health
exposure: An SSRI taken before a single dose of MDMA (study conditions: citalopram 40 mg by infusion over 90 minutes, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg by mouth; paroxetine 20 mg a day for 3 days, then MDMA 100 mg on day 3)
comparator: The same people given a dummy treatment before MDMA, and (citalopram study) dummy before dummy and citalopram alone
outcome: Rated altered-state and mood scales, euphoria and liking ratings, heart rate, blood pressure, pupil width, body temperature, and (paroxetine study only) blood concentrations of MDMA and its metabolite HMMA
magnitude: Citalopram, 16 people (Liechti et al., 2000): altered-state item clusters, percent of maximum, MDMA alone against citalopram then MDMA: positive basic mood 40.1 against 16.4, derealization 32.7 against 12.6, thought disorder 24.8 against 8.6, changed meaning of percepts 37.3 against 14.1 (ten of the 13 raised clusters lowered, three not); interactions F(1,15) 22.47 for oceanic boundlessness and 23.04 for anxious ego dissolution; no blood levels. Paroxetine, 12 men (Farre et al., 2007): peak systolic pressure 12 mm Hg lower (P=0.001), pupil widening 3.33 to 1.23 mm (P<0.001), temperature rise 0.3 C lower (P=0.041), euphoria scale peak 7.27 to 4; MDMA peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and exposure to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L (both P<0.01); HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and exposure 1189.47 against 1923.32 (both P<0.01); the paper's text gives MDMA +16 percent (peak) and +22 percent (exposure), HMMA -49 percent and -39 percent. Editors' calculation from the printed means: citalopram clusters 55 to 80 percent lower (the authors say about 60 percent overall); HMMA exposure -38 percent. Fluoxetine, 8 people, as summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022): liking 31.2, 'high' 47.6 and 'stimulated' 40.1 percent lower (P<.05).

evidence.locator: Materials and Method › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Substances and Dosing, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Study Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 514-515)
evidence.extracted: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person study of 16 volunteers (12 men and 4 women, aged 21 to 39) in four counterbalanced conditions at least 14 days apart: placebo then placebo, citalopram then placebo, placebo then MDMA, citalopram then MDMA. Citalopram 40 mg (or saline) was infused over 90 minutes, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg, SD 10) was taken by mouth, and ratings were made 120 minutes after MDMA. Six volunteers had tried recreational drugs before: two ecstasy, three a hallucinogen and one both. Editors' count: 3 of the 16 had tried ecstasy and 13 had not.

MDMA raised all three altered-state scales against placebo (Rao R(3,12)=7.25, P<.005) and citalopram pretreatment lowered them (pretreatment by treatment: oceanic boundlessness F(1,15)=22.47, anxious ego dissolution F(1,15)=23.04, visionary restructuralization F(1,15)=12.80). Item clusters, percent of maximum, MDMA alone against citalopram then MDMA: positive basic mood 40.1 against 16.4, derealization 32.7 against 12.6, thought disorder 24.8 against 8.6, changed meaning of percepts 37.3 against 14.1; of the 15 item clusters, MDMA significantly raised 13, and citalopram significantly lowered 10 of those 13 but not frightening derealization, synesthesia or facilitated recollection. Editors' calculation from the printed means: the ten lowered clusters fell by about 55 to 80 percent.

evidence.locator: Results, last paragraph (p. 516); Figure 2 (p. 518); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 517) and the paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (pp. 518-519)
evidence.extracted: On the mood scales, citalopram lowered the MDMA-induced rises in self-confidence (P<.04) and extroversion (P<.01) to the level of citalopram alone, and efficiency-activation (P<.03); the fall in heightened mood did not reach significance (P=.06), and the rises in emotional excitability and sensitivity were not lowered at all. Citalopram alone lowered some scale scores against placebo, which the authors put down mostly to its side effects (fatigue, headache and nausea; nausea in 6 of 16).

evidence.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 515); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Another interesting finding' and the continuation of the paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (p. 519)
evidence.extracted: MDMA's subjective effect lasted a mean of 3 hours; after citalopram it was markedly reduced but lasted a mean of 5 hours, stated without a method, spread or test. No blood concentrations were taken. The authors put the lowering at about 60 percent and note that all received the same 40 mg whatever their weight, with no correlation between dose per kilogram and the size of the lowering; in a pilot, two people given 60 or 80 mg of citalopram had MDMA's effects blocked to a degree comparable with 40 mg.

evidence.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Study Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 955)
evidence.extracted: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 12 healthy men (mean age 24; all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; MDMA taken on at least 5 earlier occasions). Two 3-day sessions 15 days apart: paroxetine 20 mg a day or placebo on days 1 to 3, with MDMA 100 mg on day 3, 3 hours after that day's capsule. A 13th man withdrew after two paroxetine doses (insomnia, restlessness, anxiety) and never took MDMA.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 957); Results › Physiological Effects and Subjective Effects (p. 957); Figs. 1 to 3 (pp. 958-960)
evidence.extracted: Paroxetine lowered MDMA's effects: peak systolic pressure 12 mm Hg lower (Emax F=22.20, P=0.001), diastolic 5 mm Hg and heart rate 14 beats/min lower, pupil widening from 3.33 to 1.23 mm (F=70.35, P<0.001), temperature rise 0.3 C lower (P=0.041); ARCI euphoria scale (morphine-benzedrine group) peak 7.27 to 4; VESSPA anxiety 5.55 to 2.7, sociability 3.0 to 0.58, activity 5.91 to 1.21; visual-analogue 'stimulated', 'high', 'any effect', 'good effects' and 'liking' lower (all P=0.003 or less at peak). By Table 1 the diastolic area (P=0.613) and peak (P=0.213) and the heart-rate area (P=0.093) were not significant.

evidence.locator: Results › Plasma Concentrations of MDMA and HMMA (pp. 957-958); Table 2 (p. 961)
evidence.extracted: MDMA with paroxetine against placebo (n=12): peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and area to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L, both P<0.01; HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and area 1189.47 against 1923.32, half-life 13.10 against 9.54 hours (all P<0.01); MDMA half-life 8.34 against 7.88 hours. The paper's own text gives MDMA 22 (exposure) and 16% (peak) higher and HMMA 39 (exposure) and 49% (peak) lower. Editors' calculation from the printed means: HMMA exposure -38%.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 954); Table 1 and Results › Subjective Effects (p. 957); Discussion, final paragraph (pp. 961-962)
evidence.extracted: Ratings of bad effects, fear, and depression or sadness did not change significantly with paroxetine, and no hallucinations, psychotic symptoms or serious adverse events were seen. The authors write that the marked decrease in positive effects may lead to higher MDMA doses (they give people with depression who take SSRIs as an example) and so to potentially life-threatening toxicity; no extra MDMA was given in the study, so this is their inference. The abstract gives the rise in MDMA level as 30%, a figure taken in the Discussion from an earlier 7-man analysis; the trial's own figures are 16% (peak) and 22% (exposure to 21 hours).
evidence.quote: could lead users to take higher doses of MDMA

evidence.extracted: The authors write that a single recreational dose of MDMA inhibits CYP2D6 rapidly and completely whereas several prescription doses of paroxetine are needed, that citalopram and paroxetine block the positive effects of MDMA, and that people taking an SSRI together with multiple doses of MDMA should know that the metabolism of both substances is compromised, with a possible increase in the risk of acute adverse effects already reported for poor metabolizers. The reference given for people taking SSRIs to change MDMA's effects is a rat study. No SSRI was given with MDMA in this study.

evidence.locator: Table 6, citalopram, fluoxetine and paroxetine rows; Results › MDMA › Serotonin reuptake inhibitors and MDMA, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Second-hand summary. SSRIs lowered the rated and measured effects of MDMA. Citalopram (n=16): oceanic boundlessness about 60% lower, anxious ego dissolution about 63% lower (both p<.05), heart rate 12.3% lower at 60 minutes (p<.05), acute complaints about 46% lower (p<.01). Fluoxetine (n=8; Tancer and Johanson, 2006, not read): drug liking 31.2%, 'high' 47.6% and 'stimulated' 40.1% lower (all p<.05), heart rate 14.6% lower (p<.05). Paroxetine (n=12): liking about 62%, 'high' about 68% (p<.001), systolic pressure about 41% (p<.001) and heart rate about 42% lower (p<.05). The review summarizes this as 30 to about 80% lower subjective effects and, for physiological effects, about 6 to 14% lower (about 40 to 60% for paroxetine), and says that with fluoxetine and paroxetine, both strong CYP2D6 blockers, plasma MDMA was increased despite the attenuated effects (Table 6 gives no blood-level figure for fluoxetine). Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Considerations for future research, 1st paragraph; Table 5
evidence.extracted: No trial gave an SSRI or SNRI for months to people who take one as treatment: participants were young healthy adults given the medicine once or, rarely, for up to 14 days (the longest, escitalopram with psilocybin; for MDMA 3 to 11 days: paroxetine 3, fluoxetine 5 to 11), some by the less common intravenous route (citalopram). The authors write that no serious adverse effects of these combinations were observed in clinical trial settings and that, because the trials show smaller physiological effects, the odds of serotonin syndrome may be reduced at least with acute SSRI dosing (their inference, not tested); they also write that modern MDMA-therapy trials either excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first.

risk_of_bias.note: Both studies are rated 'some concerns' on the RoB 2 crossover checklist (study cards): about 32 and 45 outcomes tested without correction, ratings that partial unblinding (side effects, obvious MDMA effects) could shift, no blood levels in the citalopram study, an unclear day-3 baseline in the paroxetine study. One level, not two, because the physiological and blood-level results do not depend on the blind.

inconsistency.note: Two groups in two countries agree in direction, as does the fluoxetine trial as summarized.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for healthy volunteers, one infusion or 3 days of an SSRI, and one fixed MDMA amount, and says that people on long-term treatment were not studied.

imprecision.note: 16 and 12 people; no confidence intervals for the differences in effect.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomized or counterbalanced within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give low. Status replicated: two independent laboratories, using different SSRIs and different measures, show the same lowering of effects; the rise in MDMA level rests on the paroxetine study alone, because the citalopram study took no blood samples. The claim states what was measured and what was not (no study gave more MDMA, none treated people for long); it gives no advice on amounts. Anchors from the review are second-hand and marked as such.

verification.flag_note: Review-only statements are marked 'as summarized'. No reference record exists for Tancer and Johanson (2006, fluoxetine; DOI not captured). MAOI evidence (Vuori 2003, Silins 2007) is with reader 55 and is not used here. The paroxetine paper's abstract states a 30% rise in MDMA; the trial's own figures are 16% and 22%. The editor may join this claim with the claim on other antidepressants.
